1.pericope_label: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters: I will make an everlasting covenant with you, the sure mercies of David

schools.summary: Reads the invitation as addressed in pity to the bereaved woman of the preceding chapter, guards the verb buy from being taken commercially, and takes the covenant for the new covenant completing the one made with David.

Follows the Jewish commentators in directing the call to the Gentiles, catalogues what the thirst is for, and refers the giving of the witness to an act past in eternity when Christ was appointed Mediator.

Reports a Jewish reading of water, wine and milk as law and wisdom, glosses buying as receiving what is freely given, and identifies the everlasting covenant with the covenant sacrifice pointed out from the beginning.
Widens the invitation to whoever can be gathered from the highways and hedges, sends the hearer to the quays where foreign goods are landed, and makes thirst both the one condition and itself a gift.

positions.view: the Gentiles, whose conversion is plainly spoken of in the chapter
all comers, not the Jews only but whoever can be picked up out of the highways and hedges, since the covenant excludes none who do not exclude themselves
the bereaved and afflicted woman of the preceding chapter, addressed in a tone of pity

debates.question: Who is the witness given to the peoples?

positions.view: the Messiah, the giving referring to an act past in eternity when Christ was appointed to the office of Mediator
the David last mentioned, that is, Christ
read rather I gave: the words refer primarily to the historic David, and are realised fully only in the one afterwards called the faithful and true witness

outliers.reading: Alone defends the verb buy against itself, observing that no silver can purchase what is offered, that something is nevertheless required so the word remains right, and that the price is simply the self-surrender which accepts the blessing.

Alone reads the waters commercially, sending the hearer to the quays and wharfs where foreign goods are landed, and adding that such goods would have stayed foreign for ever had Christ not brought in an everlasting righteousness.

themes: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David.
Behold, I have given him for a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the people.
Behold, thou shalt call a nation that thou knowest not, and nations that knew not thee shall run unto thee because of the Lord thy God, and for the Holy One of Israel; for he hath glorified thee.

6.pericope_label: Seek ye the LORD while he may be found: for my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways

schools.summary: Makes the offer conditional and time-limited, names the human thoughts the verse contradicts, and grounds the appeal on a heaven-wide difference between God's ways and the labyrinthine ways of men.

Distinguishes two senses of the way that must be forsaken, the man's chosen course and his own method of saving himself by works, and works out at length how divine and human thoughts differ in quality rather than in kind.
Reports a Jewish rendering that turns the temporal clauses into causal ones, narrows the higher thoughts to God's readiness to pardon, and suspects a lost particle of comparison in the closing verse.

Divides the summons into seeking and calling, holds that the day of grace can close within this life when the heart is incurably hardened, and requires repentance to change the mind as well as the way.

debates.question: Does while he may be found set a time limit, or give a reason?

positions.view: a reason: seek him because he may be found and call because he is near, repenting before death, after which there is no conversion of the soul
a limit: the blessings are not unconditional, and a time may come when too late is written across every effort to recover a forfeited inheritance
a limit, meaning the day of grace while mercy is still offered
both sides of it: now his patience waits and his Spirit strives, but a day comes when he is afar off, and it may come within this life when the heart is incurably hardened

debates.question: What is the force of my thoughts are not your thoughts?

positions.view: a comparison of quality more than of nature: man's thoughts are finite, evil and vain, God's infinite and holy
it answers both the promise and the warning, contradicting the notions that God's gifts can be bought with money and that the market is always open
it is about pardon: we are slow to forgive one who injures us often, while God is ready to forgive all penitents however many their sins
it sets God's ways against the despairing thoughts of men and their aimless labyrinthine ways

outliers.reading: Alone insists that the forsaking must reach the mind as well as the conduct, since it is not enough to break off evil practices without entering a caveat against evil thoughts.

Alone suspects a textual defect at the comparison of the heavens, holding that the particle of comparison has been lost through its likeness to the particle immediately before it, on the authority of all the ancient versions and a nearly identical psalm.

themes: Seek ye the Lord while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near:
Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the Lord.
For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.

10.pericope_label: As the rain cometh down and returneth not thither: so shall my word be, and ye shall go out with joy

schools.summary: Finds the whole apparatus of the agricultural parables already present in the figure, and locates the point of the comparison in the predominance of fertility rather than in irresistible force.
Offers the word as either Christ the eternal Word who returned to heaven not empty or the word of promise, and reads the thorn and brier as wicked men replaced by good.
Narrows the promises to the pardon of the greatest sinners, supplies a classical parallel for the singing hills, and reports the moral sense the old Aramaic version gives the thorn and the fir.

debates.question: Where does the point of the comparison lie?

positions.view: in energy: the likeness is the force with which the word is realised, and the word of redemption will be fulfilled irresistibly

in proportion: fertility predominates in nature despite partial or apparent failures, which pledges a like triumph in the long run; it does not exclude the partial or even total failure of many, but asserts that the saved are more than the lost

debates.question: What is the word that goes forth from the mouth?

positions.view: either Christ the eternal Word, who came down as rain and returned not empty, or else the word of promise; the choice is left open
the promises, and specifically those concerning the pardon of the greatest sinners

outliers.reading: Alone draws the consequence of his reading without softening it, that the comparison allows the partial or even total failure of many and claims only that the saved outnumber the lost.

Alone turns aside to complain that a conjunction attested by many manuscripts and every ancient version was left in the margin rather than the text, remarking that the best reading is very often found there.

themes: For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater:
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.
Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the Lord for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off.
